data.title: 'She's living the dream': My stepmother said I can buy my childhood home for $850,000. Is she taking advantage of me?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'My late father bought our house for $250,000 in the 1990s'

"She said if my dad wanted me to have it, he should have arranged that before he died." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My late father bought our house for $250,000 in the 1990s. By the time he died, it was worth about $850,000, mostly because it's spacious and in a good neighborhood. He left it to my stepmother, whom he married a few years after my mom died. She is now 74. They were together for 18 years. She took care of him through the whole illness, which I don't take lightly.

Dad told me more than once that the house would be mine someday. My stepmother now wants to sell and move somewhere smaller. She's living the dream in Miami. I offered $700,000. That's $200,000 under market, but I thought it was fair, given that she would skip agent fees and it would be a quick, clean sale. I'd have to stretch to do it, but I could manage.

She was really offended, and she told me as much. She said she's paid the property taxes and the repairs for years (she put a new roof on in 2021). She also said she spent a big chunk of her own savings on my father's care and that the house is basically her retirement plan, and that she can't just hand me $200,000 because I'm sentimental.

Don't miss: My wife says we can't afford to retire. I vetoed her $8,000 trip to Italy. We're in our 60s and have $4 million. Do I keep working?

The $200,000 discount

That's a fair point, and I told her so. What I can't get past is that a few years ago she gave her daughter $200,000 toward a house, and that is how (and why) I came up with the $200,000 haircut on my father's home. I brought that up, and she said things were different then, and pointed out that I have a good job and can buy my own place.

She said if my dad wanted me to have it, he should have arranged that before he died. As my girlfriend at the time said, "Yes, she really went there." That comment really stung. He trusted her with everything, and it feels like his wishes just evaporated. She says she honored him by caring for him and that I'm discounting everything she sacrificed.

I could, of course, walk away and buy somewhere else. I've even looked at a couple of listings. But it wouldn't be the same, and I'd always feel like the house slipped away from our family. I know that my stepsister's place has a sauna in the basement, and I'd bet anything that my stepmother helped pay for that too. Not that I'm keeping score. (OK, I know I am a little.)

Am I being unreasonable?

The Stepson

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My wife never went back to work after raising our kids. Do I have to share my retirement savings 50/50?

You can't force someone to sell you a house that never legally belonged to you.

Dear Stepson,

Don't allow steam from your stepsister's sauna to cloud your vision. You can grieve the loss of your childhood home without assigning blame.

What's more, you can't force someone to sell you a house that never belonged to you in the first place. Your childhood home, legally and morally, belonged to your father. Even though you grew up there, that doesn't give you the right to a life estate or a $200,000 discount on the purchase price because your stepmother gave her daughter $200,000 toward the down payment on her own home. What's more, selling a house to a family member below fair market value can create a gift of equity equal to the price difference, which the IRS may treat as a taxable gift.

Your late father made a promise that he did not keep, could not keep or decided not to keep. That was his responsibility. It's not your stepmother's job to make good on your father's promises. Whether he made a will leaving her the house or whether she inherited the house through state intestate laws, the end result is the same: She legally owns the house, and she has the right to live there or sell it to whomever she wants.

It is your belief that your father's wishes "evaporated." But wishes, promises and/or intentions evolve, and perhaps he realized that he wanted to take care of his wife of nearly two decades, and die with the knowledge that she would always have a roof over her head. It would have been better to have discussed those plans with you rather than leaving you in a kind of limbo, wondering if he truly wanted to leave his estate to his wife. Chances are, he did.

That does not mean this is an easy or pleasant situation for you. You have an emotional attachment to this property, and you regard your stepmother as an interloper, inheriting a property where your own mother probably once lived. It's a tough break for you and your siblings, if you have any. You made your stepmother an offer and she declined. She may be thinking about her own retirement and financial future.

Don't miss: 'I don't feel sorry for myself': I'm 64 and will be renting for the rest of my life. Is that so bad?

Passing judgment

Two decades is a long time to spend with someone. She met your father when she was in her 50s, and she's now rightly concerned about medical costs, if she needs nursing home care, especially if she does not have long-term care insurance, or any other kind of life insurance. This house may be the only asset she has, and downsizing will give her a cushion as she heads towards her 80th birthday in six years. That's quite a reality check.

I'm heartened that you realize that taking care of your father was no small deal for your stepmother. Who will take care of her if she sells you this house for $650,000 and runs out of money? Will you drive her to hospital appointments and spend hours a day with her, making sure that she takes her medication and pays her bills, and has enough to eat? That might sound dramatic, but getting older often comes with health complications.

One could argue that you both "went there." She "went there" by telling you your father wanted her to have his house. You "went there" by using emotional leverage, whether or not you believe it in your heart to be valid, to persuade her to sell this house to you on the cheap. By doing so, you are, whether you realize it or not, also passing judgment on her marriage of 18 years to a man she probably loved very much. You both spoke plainly. That's OK. Just know it's 50/50.

If you want this house, put in an offer when it is listed for sale. If she does get more than one offer and, say, one party offers $50,000 more, she may still decide to sell you the house (and maybe not even mention that she is selling it to you at less than the other offer). Remember, if she gets $950,000 rather than $850,000 - a real possibility if it's a cash buyer and it's a sought-after neighborhood - she would have been giving you a $300,000 discount if she agreed to your proposal.

All is fair in love, second marriages, legal beneficiaries and real estate. Just don't overstretch yourself financially for the sake of nostalgia.

Related: 'People in the U.S. need to wake up': As a mortgage loan officer, I rejected applications from wealthy couples. Here's why.

Check out The Moneyist's private Facebook group, where members help answer life's thorniest money issues. Post your questions, weigh in on the latest Moneyist columns or email The Moneyist at qfottrell@marketwatch.com.

data.title: Commercial HVAC Expert Brian Sinkler of Green Bay, WI Stresses Pre-Summer Inspection for HelloNation
data.description:
Commercial HVAC Expert Brian Sinkler of Green Bay, WI Stresses Pre-Summer Inspection for HelloNation

Commercial HVAC Expert Brian Sinkler of Green Bay, WI Stresses Pre-Summer Inspection for HelloNation

PR Newswire

GREEN BAY, Wis., Oct. 23, 2026

GREEN BAY, Wis., Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What is the one hvac check every business should complete before summer begins? A HelloNation article provides the answer, pointing to refrigerant levels, coil cleaning, and airflow testing as the foundation of preventive maintenance. The feature highlights Green Bay professional Brian Sinkler of Sinkler Heating and Cooling, Inc., who explains how a pre-summer inspection protects commercial hvac systems from strain, breakdowns, and rising energy costs. Readers can review the full details in a HelloNation article.

The article notes that commercial hvac systems are among the hardest-working pieces of equipment in a business. They operate for long hours every day, keeping staff and customers comfortable regardless of conditions outside. Summer creates the greatest challenge, with higher temperatures and humidity pushing systems to their limits. Without preventive maintenance, this demand can quickly turn into failure.

Checking refrigerant levels is the most important step. Refrigerant absorbs indoor heat and releases it outdoors. The HelloNation article explains that low refrigerant levels prevent proper cooling, forcing longer cycles and higher energy costs. Running with insufficient refrigerant also strains the compressor, one of the most expensive components to replace. Detecting and correcting this issue before summer helps avoid poor performance and costly repairs.

Coil cleaning is another critical part of a pre-summer inspection. Evaporator and condenser coils collect dirt and debris, which blocks heat transfer. According to the HelloNation article, when coils are coated, the system works harder to cool, raising utility bills and wearing down parts. Professional coil cleaning restores efficiency, ensuring the system operates at full capacity during peak heat.

Airflow testing completes the foundation. Blocked ducts, weak fans, or clogged filters prevent conditioned air from reaching all parts of the building. This creates uneven comfort and forces the system to run longer, wasting energy. The HelloNation article shows how airflow testing identifies these issues and ensures smooth circulation throughout the property.

Preventive maintenance avoids breakdowns at the busiest time of year. For retail businesses, warm conditions may drive customers away. Offices lose productivity when staff cannot work in comfortable conditions. Companies storing perishable goods face even greater risks from cooling failures. A pre-summer inspection ensures reliable performance when cooling is most critical.

Energy costs are another major factor. The HelloNation article stresses that commercial properties face their highest energy bills during peak summer. By confirming refrigerant levels, completing coil cleaning, and performing airflow testing, businesses reduce energy costs while improving results. These savings provide a return on investment month after month.

The article also highlights how preventive maintenance extends equipment lifespan. Motors, fans, and compressors suffer under strain when systems are neglected. Small issues left unchecked can accelerate wear and shorten useful life. By addressing them early, businesses avoid premature replacement and the high expense of new equipment.

Another advantage is avoiding emergency repair calls during peak demand. When cooling fails in the middle of summer, service technicians are in short supply. Delays and higher repair costs often follow. A pre-summer inspection provides peace of mind, reducing the chance of emergencies and securing reliable operation ahead of time.

For larger commercial buildings, inspections often include thermostat calibration, zoning system checks, and building management system adjustments. The HelloNation article explains that these steps improve energy efficiency and maintain comfort across multiple zones. Properly tuned controls allow businesses to manage costs while delivering consistent conditions throughout the property.

Some businesses view maintenance as an expense, but the article emphasizes the opposite. Preventive maintenance is an investment that lowers long-term costs. Skipping a pre-summer inspection often leads to higher energy bills, emergency service fees, and lost revenue from downtime. In contrast, scheduled service ensures stability, efficiency, and consistent comfort.

The HelloNation feature concludes that summer strain on commercial hvac systems is unavoidable, but breakdowns are not. With refrigerant levels checked, coil cleaning performed, and airflow testing completed, businesses can depend on their systems through the hottest months. Preventive maintenance delivers comfort, lowers energy costs, and protects operations.

In Green Bay, HVAC Expert Brian Sinkler of Sinkler Heating and Cooling, Inc. helps businesses prepare for these challenges. His approach to preventive maintenance aligns with the HelloNation article, stressing the value of preparation, efficiency, and reliability in commercial hvac service.

For the full feature, read The One HVAC Check Every Business Needs Before Summer. The article highlights the expertise of HVAC Expert Brian Sinkler of Green Bay and his practical advice through HelloNation.

About HelloNation
HelloNation is a premier media platform that connects readers with trusted professionals and businesses across various industries. Through its innovative "edvertising" approach that blends educational content and storytelling, HelloNation delivers expert-driven articles that inform, inspire, and empower. Covering topics from home improvement and health to business strategy and lifestyle, HelloNation highlights leaders making a meaningful impact in their communities.

data.title: BioVid Launches Mimetics™, AI Research Audiences Built on How Physicians Reason and Decide
data.description:
BioVid Launches Mimetics™, AI Research Audiences Built on How Physicians Reason and Decide

BioVid Launches Mimetics™, AI Research Audiences Built on How Physicians Reason and Decide

PR Newswire

BRISTOL, Pa., Oct. 23, 2026

Modeling physician response patterns and behavior, showing an 80–90% match with real physicians on content, reasoning, and emotion. 

BRISTOL, Pa., Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- BioVid, a life science consultancy, today announced the launch of BioVid Mimetics™, a research platform that gives pharmaceutical teams mimetics: synthetic physician audiences modeled on how those audiences reason and decide. Its respondent models are grounded in BioVid's proprietary MindSet Modeling™ program, large-scale, multi-specialty surveys of practicing physicians that measure the mindsets shaping how they process information, make judgments, and decide. The models are aligned with secondary data on clinical practice, moving beyond generic AI role-play to model the decision logic behind treatment choices.

 Like a mimetic drug, each BioVid mimetic is tested against the original: real physicians.

Prescribing data shows what physicians choose, not why. Pharma teams now face more of those "why" questions than research budgets and timelines can absorb. BioVid Mimetics™ applies the social and behavioral science of clinical judgment to model how physicians interpret evidence, weigh benefit against risk, and decide when they know enough to act.

The name comes from pharmacology, where a mimetic earns trust by doing the work of the original molecule. Every BioVid mimetic is tested against that standard, bringing the firm's long-standing commitment to science-based research to a new method.

"At BioVid, we've always believed that better commercial decisions start with a deeper understanding of human behavior," said Peggy Hirtle, CEO of BioVid. "Our goal was never simply faster or cheaper respondents. It was to reflect how physicians actually reason, with the same scientific rigor clients already trust from BioVid. Mimetics is a new way to put human understanding to work, never a replacement for it."

"A synthetic respondent can sound right and still reason wrong. The real test is whether it reasons the way the audience does," said Marco Barcella, Executive Director, Product & Technology at BioVid. "Where the decision warrants, we run the same study with a human cohort and a mimetic cohort and compare the findings, the reasoning, and the mental and emotional responses directly. Clients see where mimetic findings hold and where human research should lead."

In BioVid's validation work to date, mimetic and human cohorts have shown an 80% to 90% match on content, reasoning, and emotion across thousands of parallel tests.

BioVid Mimetics™ is available off the shelf or tailored with a client's own primary research. It supports message and concept testing, positioning, drivers and barriers, segmentation, and opportunity assessment, and includes:

Mimetic Respondents: Mimetic or hybrid studies, with mimetic fieldwork complete in one to two weeks after receipt of required inputs, followed by a full report and readout from BioVid's research team.

Mimetic Segments App: Segments that client teams question directly, share materials with, and return to between research waves.

Client Customization: Models tailored with a client's own research, segment profiles, and CRM data, exclusive to that client and firewalled from all others.

To learn more, visit www.biovid.com/mimetics. 

About BioVid

BioVid is a life science consultancy applying behavioral science and AI to commercial and market access strategy. Its offerings include the CIAIRA™ AI platform, Tumor Worlds™, and BioVid Mimetics™. BioVid is a recognized leader in new product demand estimation, commercial communication optimization, and customer and patient segmentation research.

Visit www.biovid.com.

data.title: The real test for Moderna's cancer vaccine isn't about beating Keytruda. It's keeping cancer from coming back in the long term.
data.description:
By Jaimy Lee

The first Phase 3 data for a cancer vaccine has raised questions about whether a potential new treatment is worth it

Moderna's stock was down slightly Friday, after plunging 17.6% on Thursday.

Moderna and Merck proved their custom cancer vaccine cut the risk of melanoma returning for longer than the cancer drug Keytruda, but it may take several years to understand if a therapeutic vaccine is better at beating the disease than immunotherapies.

The companies on Thursday released the highly anticipated Phase 3 data for intismeran, showing that a combination of the experimental vaccine and Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of the cancer returning or the patient passing away by 42% after about two years compared to patients only taking Keytruda.

Though a seemingly striking outcome, the vaccine wasn't as efficacious as some investors had hoped. But the real test of intismeran will be how well the vaccine keeps cancer at bay over time. If it's successful, the custom treatment could radically change how certain patients with cancer are treated.

For now, however, the reaction to the data has been mixed. The study's results were unexpectedly released two days early as a result of a broken embargo, sending down the shares of both companies. Moderna's stock (MRNA) plummeted by as much as 25% on Thursday afternoon to close 17.6% lower. Merck's shares (MRK) closed 1.7% lower.

By Friday afternoon, Moderna's stock was off 2%, while Merck's shares were down 1.6%.

Analysts speculated that the haphazard way that the Phase 3 results came out may have rattled investors. Investors are also asking broader questions about whether a brand-new technology like intismeran is as game-changing as it's promised to be, especially when compared to neoadjuvant immunotherapy, which is the practice of giving Keytruda and other immunotherapies to patients before they go through surgery to have their tumors removed.

"While approval seems likely, commercial success is far less certain," RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh told investors on Thursday. "The data raises fundamental questions about [intismeran's] value proposition relative to standards of care, particularly neoadjuvant immunotherapy, which produces similar efficacy at potentially much less cost."

Keytruda is often given to patients after surgery to prevent the return of their cancer, but sometimes it's administered to patients in advance of surgery to shrink the tumor.

A study published in 2023 found that giving Keytruda to patients with melanoma before surgery significantly extended how long they lived until the cancer came back or spread, or until the patient died, compared to those who received it after surgery. A Phase 3 trial of Yervoy and Opdivo, both of which are immunotherapies owned by Bristol Myers Squibb (BMY), had a similar outcome when given to patients with late-stage melanoma before surgery.

Both studies, however, were done in patients with clinically detectable Stage 3 cancer. That's how the doctors knew to administer the treatment before surgery. But the patients enrolled in the intismeran trial didn't know what stage of cancer they had until after they had surgery, according to Daniel Olson, an oncologist in the UChicago Medicine hospital system, which is one of the sites for other intismeran studies.

"People are saying, 'What's the value of an mRNA vaccine if you can just give [Keytruda] neoadjuvantly?'" he said. "Well, these patients, you can't."

Other analysts also questioned whether comparing studies with different patient populations is fair game.

"While we're not sure this is the right comparison, we see signs [intismeran and Keytruda] have a more durable effect," Jefferies analysts wrote in a note on Friday.

That's the big hope for intismeran, which is a therapeutic vaccine. Experts believe that the protective qualities that we associate with vaccines will work in cancer, hopefully creating lasting stretches of time before cancer comes back than what the currently available drugs can offer.

Intismeran works by training a patient's immune system to respond to the neoantigens in their tumor and then attack any residual cancer cells, according to Jane Healy, Merck's head of oncology early clinical development who ran the Phase 1 study for intismeran.

She believes that's why there was no difference between the patients who got the vaccine and those who got Keytruda in the first six months of the Phase 3 study. It takes time for the immune system to be trained, and for Healy, that means the benefits of a therapeutic vaccine will come later.

"It lends to the durability that [Keytruda] is going in and activating the immune system," she said in an interview. "But [intismeran] is training the immune system in what to recognize."

In the Phase 2 study for the vaccine, the hazard ratio - an important metric for understanding how well a new treatment performs compared to another drug or placebo - was 0.56 after about two years. But the most up-to-date data shows that the hazard ratio didn't degrade much over time, which commonly happens after experimental therapies move from smaller Phase 2 trials into larger Phase 3 studies. It was 0.51 after five years.

"The longer-term data from the Phase 2 - the five years - showing durable responses in these patients out to five years makes me hopeful that this new class of therapies is capable of this durable benefit," Healy said, later adding: "I'm hopeful that we're going to finally see that long-term benefit of vaccines that we get in infectious disease playing out in the oncology setting."

-Jaimy Lee

What Should Better Home & Finance Holding Company Investors Know After 28.5% Stock Drop? The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz Outlines Securities Fraud Class Action Lead Plaintiff Deadline

PR Newswire

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 23, 2026

Lawsuit alleges Better Home & Finance Holding Company made misleading statements to investors from March 13, 2026 to May 7, 2026; lead plaintiff motions are due November 20, 2026

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz today announced a class action lawsuit against Better Home & Finance Holding Company ("Better Home & Finance" or the "Company") (NASDAQ: BETR) on behalf of investors who acquired the Company's securities from March 13, 2026 to May 7, 2026. Filed on September 21, 2026, the case is Gastwirt v. Better Home & Finance Holding Company, et al., U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, Case No. 1:26-cv-08219.

If you lost money on Better Home & Finance Holding Company securities, submit your Better Home & Finance Holding Company loss information by November 20, 2026 to learn about participating in the lawsuit.

Better Home & Finance Holding Company class action timeline

  • Class period begins: March 13, 2026
  • Class period ends: May 7, 2026
  • Complaint filed: September 21, 2026
  • Lead plaintiff motion deadline: November 20, 2026

What happened?

On May 7, 2026, Better Home released its first quarter 2026 financial results, disclosing that its previously announced target of reaching $1.0 billion in monthly funded loan volume appeared likely to be deferred due, in part, to borrower hesitation in a higher-rate environment.

On this news, Better Home's stock price fell $12.17, or 28.5%, to close at $30.52 per share on May 7, 2026, thereby injuring investors.

What is the Better Home & Finance Holding Company lawsuit about?

The Better Home & Finance Holding Company securities lawsuit alleges that, between March 13, 2026 and May 7, 2026, defendants made materially false and/or misleading statements and failed to disclose material adverse facts about Better Home & Finance Holding Company's business, operations, and prospects. Specifically, the complaint alleges defendants failed to disclose that: (1) the Company's conversion funnel was already slowing due to macro factors; (2) as a result, the Company's $1 billion monthly funded volume target was likely to be deferred; and (3) as a result, defendants' positive statements about Better Home & Finance Holding Company's business, operations, and prospects were materially misleading and/or lacked a reasonable basis.

"According to the complaint filed against Better Home & Finance Holding Company, the Company, among other things, did not disclose that the Company's conversion funnel was already slowing due to macro factors. The November 20, 2026 deadline is a key date for Better Home & Finance Holding Company investors who want a voice in how this case moves forward," said Frank R. Cruz of The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz.

What should Better Home & Finance Holding Company investors do now?

The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz can help Better Home & Finance Holding Company investors evaluate potential claims to recover their losses.

Investors who want to serve as lead plaintiff in the Better Home & Finance Holding Company class action must file a motion with the Court by November 20, 2026. For more information, visit the Better Home & Finance Holding Company case page, email info@frankcruzlaw.com, or call 310-914-5007.

If you inquire by email, please include your mailing address, telephone number, and number of shares purchased.

Investors may retain counsel of their choice. Better Home & Finance Holding Company investors who bought during the class period may also take no action and remain absent class members. No class has been certified yet in the Better Home & Finance Holding Company case.

Questions and answers about the Better Home & Finance Holding Company lawsuit

Who is eligible? Investors who bought Better Home & Finance Holding Company securities between March 13, 2026 and May 7, 2026 and lost money may be class members, and may seek lead plaintiff appointment by November 20, 2026.

What does a lead plaintiff do? The lead plaintiff is appointed by the court to represent all class members and direct the Better Home & Finance Holding Company class action.

Must I be lead plaintiff to share in a recovery? No, Better Home & Finance Holding Company investors can take no action and remain absent class members.

How are attorneys' fees handled? The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz works on contingency, so investors pay no attorneys' fees unless there is a recovery, and any fees require court approval.

About The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz

The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz investigates and prosecutes securities fraud and corporate malfeasance class actions. With nearly 20 years of litigation experience, the firm focuses on complex securities class actions and gives each client personal, one-on-one attention throughout the legal process.

Prior results do not guarantee a similar outcome.

data.title: Think annuities are a rip-off? Now might be the perfect time to reconsider.
data.description:
By Philip van Doorn

Also in Weekend Reads: How to change your approach as the stock-market seesaws, some good news for home buyers, and advice from The Moneyist

Preconceived notions can keep people away from entire categories of investment vehicles that might fit in with their long-term financial goals.

Some investors steer clear of annuities, even though they can provide ballast to a portfolio or retirement security with guaranteed income.

This might be because some people don't realize that there is a variety of annuity investment products, some of which may address their specific concerns about risk, potential returns and time commitments. Something else to keep in mind is that diversification might serve you well, even with annuities, to address your money goals and lower your risk.

Beth Pinsker wrote about how most people like the idea of guaranteed income, but might not consider the best investments to fit that need.

Brett Arends presented strategies to invest in annuities as part of a larger long-term investment allocation that takes inflation into account.

Related coverage:

-- I'm 58 and hate annuities. How can I get dependable income in retirement?

-- Is your annuity really guaranteed? Read this before you buy one.

-- Americans think they'll need $5,094 a month to live comfortably in retirement. Here's how far off they are from reality.

-- The MarketWatch Picks team's guide to annuities

A tale of two stock markets

Even as the AI build-out dominates their attention, investors have been making big moves toward nontechnology sectors.

For the week through Friday at about 2 p.m. Eastern time, the S&P 500 SPX was down 0.3%, but 68% of its stocks were up. The S&P 500's information-technology sector XX:SP500.45 had declined only slightly, but the communications-services sector XX:SP500.50 was down 5.7%. The communications sector is dominated by Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG), which was down 8.8% for the week, and Meta Platforms (META), which fell 7.5% for the week.

Underscoring the recent move away from the artificial-intelligence infrastructure build-out trade, the PHLX Semiconductor Index SOX showed a one-week decline of 2.9%.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500's healthcare sector XX:SP500.35 was up 1.3% for one week and the consumer-staples sector XX:SP500.30 was rising 0.4%.

Joseph Adinolfi looked deeper into the stock market's wild swings.

Barbara Kollmeyer interviewed Max Kettner, the chief multiasset strategist at HSBC, who advised investors chasing the AI trade to speed up their reaction time.

More coverage of this week's sector action:

-- Investors' search for safety has made toothpaste stocks more expensive than tech

-- 7 healthcare stocks that stand out as investors pay up for the sector

The bond market is also churning

Early on Friday, 10-year U.S. Treasury notes BX:TMUBMUSD10Y were yielding 4.97%, as increased buying activity brought the yield down from 5.09% a week earlier. The 10-year yield peaked this year at an intraday high of 5.37% on Oct. 7. The 10-year yield was 4.17% at the end of last year.

Christine Idzelis explained how interest-rate spreads in pockets of the bond market have been showing their most dramatic moves in decades.

Tech coverage

Meta's upcoming Muse Charm device, which will work with its Muse AI agent.

Meta's stock declined as concerns over heavy spending on AI overshadowed the 26% increase in third-quarter revenue the company reported on Wednesday.

But some professional money managers have a more positive take on Meta's ability to grow new revenue streams tied to its Muse AI agent, as reported by Christine Ji and Nora Redmund.

More coverage of technology companies:

-- This wonky maneuver kept Mark Zuckerberg from fleeing a California billionaire tax

-- Why investors should be skeptical of a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger

-- SpaceX's stock made billions for college endowments. But their luck is about to run out.

-- Why a former Intel skeptic is giving up his negative call on the stock after four years

-- Tesla's stock falls as Elon Musk leaves investors wanting more

AI fallout hurts students and colleges

Hannah Pedone took a detailed look at how a decision to major in computer science, which may have seemed a sure thing for a graduate's employment prospects only a few years ago, may backfire in the current job market.

Two bits of good news for prospective home buyers

The national weekly average rate for a 30-year mortgage loan declined to 7.32% on Thursday from 7.40% the previous week, according to Freddie Mac (FMCC). Last week, the average rate was unchanged after rising for the previous seven weeks.

Meanwhile, U.S. builders cut their average price for new homes by 6% for the seventh month in a row, according to a survey by the National Association of Home Builders.

Aarthi Swaminathan reported on how some home buyers are making 7% mortgage rates work for them.

When good news on cancer treatment becomes bad news for investors

Moderna's stock is up nearly sixfold in 2026, even after a 17.5% decline on Oct. 22.

Moderna's stock (MRNA) has shot up this year to $205.88 on Friday afternoon, from $29.49 at the end of 2025. But the stock fell 17.5% on Thursday, after details of the mostly positive trial results for the company's new melanoma treatment were leaked.

Jaimy Lee spoke with industry professionals and analysts to find out why investors reacted negatively, ahead of Moderna's official release of trial study results on Saturday.

The oil flows, but gas prices stay high

The volume of crude oil (CL00) (BRN00) flowing through the Strait of Hormuz is now close to where it was before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February. Here's why gasoline prices remain high, and what we might expect for crude-oil prices heading into 2027.

More from the Commodities Corner: Silver's recent 50% drop from a record high hints that an economic slowdown looms

Advice from the Moneyist

Quentin Fottrell is The Moneyist.

This week, Quentin Fottrell - The Moneyist - attempted to mediate a dispute between a married couple, over how to allocate their cash: Should they pay down debt, or invest?

data.title: Oil markets are on edge ahead of the weekend, as midterm elections near and fresh U.S. strikes on Iran are predicted
data.description:
By Isabel Wang and Myra P. Saefong

Global oil prices are closing in on their highest levels since the Iran war began

Oil has climbed back to an Iran-war high and may soon go higher, if the U.S. and Israel strike Iran after their respective voters go to the polls in the coming days.

Eight months into the Iran war, the global energy crisis is showing no signs of easing. Instead, oil prices were surging again, hurtling toward their highest levels since the conflict began in February and stoking fears that the world is heading toward an even more punishing energy crunch.

"Worries about oil back over $100 a barrel and the Iran conflict flaring up again are top of mind heading into the weekend," said Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group.

Global Brent crude for December delivery (BRN00) (BRNZ26) jumped 3.4% to $111.44 a barrel Friday afternoon, putting the benchmark within striking distance of its wartime settlement high of $118.35, reached in late March. West Texas Intermediate crude for December delivery (CL.1) (CLZ26) also climbed 3.5% to $103.09 a barrel. It settled as high as $112.95 in April, its highest level since the Iran war began, according to FactSet data.

The recent uptick in oil prices comes as the Iran-backed Houthis conducted further drone strikes Wednesday on Saudi airports and the Saudi Aramco Shaybah oil field, attacks that earlier this week led the U.S. to order embassy staff in Riyadh to leave the country. Trump has warned that the U.S. could attack Iran anew after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and both the U.S. and Israel have been preparing options for strikes after voters go to the polls. Israel holds its elections on Tuesday.

Another risk for energy markets: Iran said that if U.S. and Israeli bombings resume, Tehran will respond with strikes on pipelines and airports in oil-rich Persian Gulf countries, according to Wall Street Journal reporting.

"Iran is agitating to keep oil prices high and push down American popular support for the Trump administration and the war," said Matt Gertken, chief geopolitical and U.S. political strategist at BCA Research. "But after the election President Trump will intensify strikes to try to coerce Iran's leaders into a ceasefire."

Trump on Thursday hinted at fresh action against Iran during a speech in Iowa.

"We're going to have Iran finished very soon," he said in Sioux City. "One way or the other, it's going to be done very soon, and your gasoline prices and your oil is going to come tumbling down."

Anna Kelly, a White House spokeswoman, said in an emailed response to MarketWatch on Friday that the U.S. will not be attacking Iran "at any time" prior to the midterm elections.

"As President Trump stated, Iran is in very bad condition, both economically and militarily, and the blockade will remain in full force and effect, with oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait," she said.

But oil's climb back toward its wartime highs is more than a geopolitical story. It's the clearest sign yet of how exposed Trump and the Republicans are to the one issue they can't spin: the price at the pump. The national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline is $4.29, according to AAA. That's up from less than $3 a gallon before the war.

It's a test not just for a stock market already juggling earnings, an upcoming interest-rate decision from the Federal Reserve and mounting worries about debt related to the artificial-intelligence build-out, but also for Trump and his party, who have staked so much on the economy ahead of a crucial moment that could shape the direction of the president's final two years in office.

Beyond a possible fresh U.S. attack on Iran, the post-midterm outlook is cloudy. Democrats appear poised to take control of at least one chamber of Congress and have pledged to try to wind down the Iran war. But they're unlikely to win enough seats to override a Trump veto of a bill that would restrict military operations, as a longtime national security expert wrote in a CNN analysis.

Trump, for his part, has taken steps to ease the pressure on energy markets, including temporarily allowing Russia to supply diesel to U.S. and other markets and announcing plans to use Defense Production Act funding to expand oil production and refining.

That move opens up money for oil projects, but it takes years to build a refinery. So really, "this is a policy for the 2030 diesel market," Giacomo Prandelli, a commodity analyst and geopolitical strategist and the writer of a newsletter called Merchant's News, said on X. Voters will soon go to the polls, and they "pay today's prices."

"The oil market isn't pricing availability alone. It's pricing reliability," said Angie Gildea, global head of oil and gas at KPMG, in comments to MarketWatch. "Even when barrels are flowing, concerns about energy infrastructure and shipping routes can keep a risk premium in prices."

With no end to the Iran conflict in sight, market analysts see oil prices staying elevated even in the aftermath of the midterms.

Brent crude could remain in the range of $110 to $120 a barrel for a while, further increasing inflation risks, said Fawad Razaqzada, global macroeconomic market analyst at StoneX Trading and Forex.com. "That in turn could be bad news for all sorts of risk assets," he told MarketWatch on Friday.

Gertken at BCA Research said consumers can handle oil prices that average $105 a barrel over the coming months, but not an increase to $160. However, should oil reach $160 a barrel, the Trump administration might try "toppling the Iranian regime," he said. "So Iran will probably not drive prices that high."

He expects to see U.S. strikes intensifying in the coming months, and then both the U.S. and Iran opting for negotiations due to a "lack of economic and political capabilities to support a longer war."

Both the U.S. and global oil benchmarks have risen for three consecutive weeks and on Friday were on pace for their biggest three-week advance since early September, according to FactSet data.

Robert Schroeder and Joy Wiltermuth contributed.

-Isabel Wang -Myra P. Saefong

data.title: Kidney Patients Back Bipartisan Bill to Expand Disability Employment
data.description:
Kidney Patients Back Bipartisan Bill to Expand Disability Employment

Kidney Patients Back Bipartisan Bill to Expand Disability Employment

PR Newswire

WASHINGTON, Oct. 23, 2026

U.S. Representatives Hoyer and Sessions Lead AbilityOne Modernization Bill

Kidney Disease and Jobs are Focus of National Disability Employment Month

WASHINGTON, Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The American Association of Kidney Patients (AAKP), the nation's oldest and largest independent kidney patient advocacy organization, today announced plans to accelerate national grassroots patient advocacy in support of bipartisan legislation that will modernize the federal AbilityOne program. The American Procurement Improvement Act (APIA), H.R. 10443, is championed by U.S. Representatives Pete Sessions (R-TX) and Steny Hoyer (D-MD). AAKP defines kidney disease as both an American healthcare and workforce issue and fights to expand career opportunities and job protections for all Americans impacted by kidney disease, disabilities, and chronic diseases.

The AbilityOne program creates private sector employment opportunities for over 41,000 Americans with severe vision and other disabilities, including nearly 3,000 American Veterans. In FY 2025, the program generated nearly 48 million direct labor hours, an 8 percent increase and a significant measure of disability employment growth, with workers working and working more hours. AbilityOne delivered more than $4.7 billion in products and services to the Federal government in FY 2025 and drew discouraged workers into the U.S. labor force while supporting greater workforce participation, increasing economic independence, and self-sufficiency. The AbilityOne mission taps the underutilized workforce of people with significant disabilities to deliver high-quality, mission-essential products and services to federal agencies, including the U.S. Department of Defense and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

The APIA legislation removes outdated statutory barriers to hiring, retention, advancement, and movement into careers of choice, including emerging fields and new lines of business. It also modernizes federal procurement by aligning AbilityOne with contemporary procurement practices and streamlines procurement processes so the program can respond faster to emerging federal agency priorities. The APIA legislation protects taxpayer interests, strengthens program accountability and stewardship by preserving oversight, transparency, and worker protections while modernizing AbilityOne Commission authorities. The legislation is seen as an opportunity to improve federal procurement and strengthen the federal government's domestic supplier base.

Over 36 million Americans live with kidney disease, over 600,000 are on dialysis, and nearly 100,000 are awaiting a kidney transplant. Further, interrelated cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic diseases have impacted more than 25% of the adult population and are a leading cause of death. More broadly, the American Heart Association estimates that 90% of U.S. adults, or about 240 million people, have some degree of interconnected cardiovascular, kidney, or metabolic health conditions. For kidney patients dependent upon status-quo, in-center hemodialysis, burdensome thrice-weekly dialysis sessions force many patients, against their own choosing, into unemployment, disability, and dependency. AAKP believes dialysis-related unemployment, and the associated costs borne by families and taxpayers, is one of the media's least-reported stories in legacy kidney care. AAKP's policy agenda focuses on transplant readiness, more opportunities for organ transplants, more flexible, patient-centered home dialysis solutions, and stronger job protections for both kidney patients and living organ donors.

AAKP President Edward V. Hickey, III, a chronic kidney disease patient, stated, "AAKP strongly endorses the American Procurement Improvement Act (APIA) and expresses our deepest gratitude to Representatives Steny Hoyer and Peter Sessions for their bipartisan leadership and commitment to Americans managing disabilities and their efforts to secure meaningful employment opportunities with solid wages. People impacted by disability and chronic diseases face tremendous hurdles to continued employment and return to the workforce - especially America's proud Veterans. This legislation reflects consensus language among stakeholders, including advocates, employers, and organized labor, and sends a very positive message, amid national economic concerns, that the voices and needs of disabled Americans and their families are heard and not forgotten by the U.S. Congress. We encourage Congress to step up and pass this legislation before the close of the year." Hickey is a U.S. Marine Corps Veteran, a former senior congressional aide, and has served in appointed roles in two presidential administrations, including the U.S. Department of Commerce (DOC) and the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM). At OPM, he was heavily involved in policy issues related to federal Veterans preference in civil service hiring and expanded federal job opportunities. He currently serves on the American Board of Internal Medicine's (ABIM) Nephrology Specialty Board and as the Chair of the AAKP Veterans Health Initiative, the largest kidney health outreach program outside of the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

October is National Disability Employment Month, and AAKP and its allies remind elected and appointed government leaders to address health and employment concerns that impact patients, families, and communities. Through multiple partnerships, AAKP leads the kidney community in providing kidney patients and transplant recipients, including Veterans, access to virtual job fairs and employment skills training opportunities. AAKP is currently sponsoring virtual job fairs, in partnership with CareerEco, on January 13, 2027, and May 18, 2027, that will service Veterans and military families. AAKP's past collaborations have included webinars with Idealist and virtual disability and Veteran hiring fairs with Bender Consulting.

AAKP Vice President and Chair of Policy and Global Affairs Paul T. Conway, a 49-year kidney patient and 29-year transplant recipient, stated, "The AbilityOne program has supported private sector employment for people managing disabilities and chronic diseases for nearly ninety years and reflects the exceptional American values of self-reliance and independence. Representatives Steny Hoyer and Pete Sessions have consistently shown respect for the creativity, talents, and skills of disabled citizens and have dedicated their public careers to expanding job opportunities in the workforce and across the federal supply chain. The American Procurement Improvement Act increases accountability for taxpayer funds and will result in more well-paying jobs for Americans whose desire and capacity to work and contribute are underappreciated." Conway is a former Chief of Staff for both the U.S. Department of Labor and the U.S. Office of Personnel Management and a former Deputy Secretary for Health and Human Resources for the Commonwealth of Virginia. He has overseen multiple federal and state disability employment, workforce training, and health service programs throughout his public career. He is the past Chair of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's Patient Engagement Advisory Committee (PEAC) and serves on the Observational Study Monitoring Board of the Kidney Precision Medicine Program (KPMP) administered by the National Institutes of Health, National Institute of Diabetes, Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIH/NIDDK).

To advance the APIA, AAKP is working with former U.S. Representative Tony Coelho, Chair of the Partnership to Improve Patient Care as well as the Alliance for Expanding America's Workforce. Along with AAKP, APIA is endorsed by over 60 national patient and disability organizations, labor unions and employers including the American Association of People with Disabilities, SEIU, Bender Consulting, National Council of SourceAmerica Employers, CEO Commission for Disability Employment, the Arc of the United States, National Organization on Disability, National Down Syndrome Society, National Disability Rights Network, National Federation of the Blind, Melwood Inc., WORK Inc., ORC Industries, Employment Source, Opportunity Center, Inc., PARC, ACHIEVE Human Services, Inc., Human Technologies, InspiriTec, PORTCO Inc, PRIDE Industries, Phoenix, Pueblo Diversified Industries, and the Association of People Supporting EmploymentFirst (APSE).

AAKP, alongside a broad and diverse coalition of patient organizations, transplant experts, and Congressional allies, is also working to secure passage of the Living Donor Protection Act (LDPA), S. 1552/H.R. 4582 and H.R. 4583, in 2026. The bipartisan bill protects living organ donors from job and insurance discrimination based solely on their decision to donate a kidney to save another life, barriers cited most often by potential organ donors. The bipartisan legislation is led by Senator Tom Cotton (R-AK) and Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY). It was voted out of the Senate HELP Committee on February 26, 2026, with full bipartisan support, the endorsement of AAKP, the larger kidney community, and the American Council of Life Insurance (ACLI).

In 2018, with bipartisan support from Congress and the Trump Administration, AAKP and transplant professionals worked with the U.S. Department of Labor's (DOL) legal team and the DOL Wage and Hour Division to have DOL issue Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) protections for living organ donors, based on the original intent of the FMLA's Congressional co-sponsors (click here to read the letter and click here to watch the video). Congressional passage of the LDPA in 2026 will codify the DOL's 2018 FMLA job protections and prohibit insurers from discriminating against living donors. Increased living organ donation, improved transplant readiness among kidney patients, and greater opportunities for transplantation have been national goals for decades and were reinforced in 2019 through the Executive Order on Advancing American Kidney Health.

Follow AAKP on social media at @kidneypatient on Facebook, @kidneypatients on X, and @kidneypatients on Instagram, and visit https://aakp.org/ for more information. AAKP patient advocates advance bipartisan kidney policy including: passage of the bipartisan law modernizing the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) (2023); lifetime transplant drug coverage for kidney patients (2020); the historic Executive Order on Advancing American Kidney Health signed by President Donald Trump (2019); job protections for living organ donors under the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) via the U.S. Department of Labor (2018); and Congressional approval of HIV positive organ transplants for HIV positive patients (2013).
